levels.text:
Welcome Aboard Captain!

Press the "Next" button below.

If you need help at any point in your journey, please visit my youtube channel to find trouble shooting steps or watch a demonstration.

[reference to channel will go here]
Before we begin lets make sure the system is working.

levels.name: Keyboard
levels.text:
Here is a Keyboard.

Press the buttons on it to make noise.

levels.name: Scope
levels.text:
These displays shows you a visual representation of the sound as you play.

Musicians call them oscilloscopes.

levels.name: Volume
levels.text: If the volume isn't loud enough use this slider.
If you CANNOT hear any sounds after turning up the volume, be sure to check your device's sound settings.
If you CAN hear sound, then click Next to learn more about navigation.
If you are using a touchscreen, then the controls should feel natural. Tap to press. Hold to move a handle.
If you are using a mouse or touchpad, notice that you don't need to grab the handle on the slider directly. As long as the handle is highlighted you can click the mouse to "grab" the handle.
You can also use the spacebar on your keyboard to activate a "grab" or a "press" action.
My personal preference is to move with the mouse and "grab" or "press" with the spacebar.
But there are several other options for navigation.

You can continue using a mouse to navigate with a cursor.

Alternatively, you can navigate with the arrow keys on a computer keyboard.
WASD keys also work.
(If you're feeling adventurous you can also try using a game controller. I frequently use an Xbox controller for this.)
While "grabbing" a slider handle with the spacebar, try using the arrow keys to adjust it's value with more precision.

Turning on caps lock allows you to play your computer keyboard like a piano.

The home row of letters
(ASDFGHJKL) are the white keys of a piano (CDEFGABCD)

If you need help, please visit my youtube channel to watch a demonstration.

[reference to channel will go here]
Once you are comfortable with the basics of navigation press the "Next" button to continue to the first topic.
Let's begin our journey into sound design.
The art of sound design can be compared to the art of mixing colors for painting.
By combining and manipulating simple sounds we can make very complex ones.
The first tool in our toolbox is the Oscillator.
Oscillators are sources of sound waves, like the strings of a guitar.

Unlike the strings of the guitar, you don't play  the oscillator directly.

Instead you use special controls to affect the oscillator.
When you play the keyboard below, it instructs the oscillator to produce specific frequencies of sound.
In American and European music, the letters "A" through "G" are used as labels for different families of frequencies.
For example, the letter "A" is used to represent the frequencies of 27.5Hz, 55Hz, 110Hz, 220Hz, 440Hz, etc.
This is similar to how we label colors of the rainbow. The family of "Red" colors includes many different shades.

The keyboard below only uses C, D, E, G, and A.

These frequencies were selected because I think they sound nice together.

When any frequency is doubled, musicians say it went up 1 Octave.

A0=27.5Hz -> A1=55Hz -> A2=110Hz

levels.name: Octave Slider
levels.text:
This is an Octave slider.

It changes how the oscillator reacts to instructions from the keyboard.
Experiment with different values to hear how it changes the sound.

levels.name: Frequency Info
levels.text:
Here is a display that tells you about the sounds you are making.

It's okay if you don't understand everything it shows right now.

levels.name: Step Sequencer
levels.text:
Here is another controller. Musicians call it a step sequencer.

It automatically plays notes for you.
Press the play button (marked with a triangle) on the step sequencer to start the sequence.
Press the "New" button to have it generate a new random sequence.
Use the speed slider to adjust how fast the sequence plays.
You can also click on the grid of squares to manually adjust note played at each step.
Explore these controls and press "Next" when you are ready for more!
Sound waves have two important properties: Frequency and Amplitude.
So far we have been focusing on Frequency. Let's turn our attention to Amplitude.
Amplitude is a fancy word for describing how big a wave is. This is true for sound waves, ocean waves, and even light waves.
When a sound wave has a large amplitude value, we say that sound is loud.
Push play on the step sequencer and then adjust the volume slider. Notice how the size of the wave displayed in the Oscilloscopes change.
Just like you have explored different ways to control Frequency, there are many ways to control Amplitude.
Here is a new panel that gives you another control over Amplitude.
The amplitude slider is controlling the oscillator. Higher settings make the waves bigger. Lower settings make the waves smaller.
Meanwhile, the volume slider is controlling a different part of the synthesizer called an amplifier.
The waves travels from the oscillator TO the amplifier.
If the amplitude of the oscillator is set to 0, then the amplifier doesn't get any waves to amplify.
If the volume setting of the amplifier is set to 0 then all of waves from the oscillator get reduced to 0.
Both need to be set above 0 in order for us to hear anything.
Explore these controls and press "Next" when you are ready for more.
Let's turn our attention back to Frequency.
The label A4 represents the frequency 440Hz. The label A5 represents the frequency 880Hz. This jump from A4 to A5, or C1 to C2, or F6 to F7, each represent a jump of 1 octave.
Every jump of 1 octave always covers a distance of exactly 12 semitones.

Like there are 12 inches in a foot, there are 12 semitones in an octave.

A4 to A5 = 12 semitones = 1 Octave
But there are other frequencies within the distance of an octave.

For example, between A4 and A5 we have frequencies labeled like:

A4, A#4, B4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, E5, F5, F#5, G5, G#5, A5
You may notice two weird things about that list.

First, the numbers change from 4 to 5 at "C".

A4, A#4, B4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, E5, F5, F#5, G5, G#5, A5

Second, some of the notes have a hashtag symbol: #

A4, A#4, B4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, E5, F5, F#5, G5, G#5, A5

The # symbol is used to indicate an increase of frequency by exactly 1 semitone.

So F#4 means: the frequency 1 semitone above F4

Some frequencies, like F and G, have a frequency placed between them. While frequencies like B and C do not.

A4, A#4, B4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, E5, F5, F#5, G5, G#5, A5

One more thing. The list repeats:

A4, A#4, B4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, E5, F5, F#5, G5, G#5, A5, A#5, B5, C6, C#6, D6, D#6, E6, F6, F#6, G6, G#6, A6, A#6, B6, C7, ...

levels.name: Semitones
levels.text: Here is a new panel. It increases all the sound waves coming out of the oscillator by the same number of semitones.
Setting it to "+1 st" (st = semitone) makes F5 become F#5 and it makes B3 become C4.
As you explore these settings, notice how the Octave and Semitone sliders combine to affect the output frequency.

G4 + 1 octave = G5

G5 - 7 semitones = C5

I have one more panel for you before we move to the next topic.

Explore these settings a bit more first, then click next to reveal it.
Here is a new control panel. Instead of a slider, it is a XY pad. This allows you to control Frequency and Amplitude at the same time.
Frequency is set to control semitones and is on the X axis. Amplitude is on the Y axis.

I recommend pushing play on the sequencer and then playing with the different controls.

There is no wrong answer.
Explore these controls and press "Next" when you are ready for the next topic!
The colors we see out in the world rarely match the "pure" colors of the rainbow.
Similarly, most sounds we hear in the world are rarely made of a single "pure" frequency.
For example, the "A" string on a guitar sounds different than the "A" string on a Cello. Even though they both produce sound waves with the A2 frequency of 110Hz.
The reason is because of something called Harmonics.
the "A" string on a guitar makes a sound wave which has many frequencies, but the A2 frequency is the one with the most amplitude.
Since the A2 frequency is the loudest, and lowest, it is called the Fundamental frequency of that string.
For short, guitarists call it the "A" string. Even though it produces many other frequencies.
All the extra frequencies produced when that "A" string is plucked are called harmonic frequencies, or harmonics for short.
Guitar strings produce different harmonics than Cello strings. That is one reason why those instruments sound different.
The oscillator in the synthesizer you are currently playing has it's own unique fingerprint of harmonic frequencies.
Synthesizers are all about designing your own sounds.
So, in addition to the oscillator, this synthesizer also happens to have something called a Filter.
Oscillators create sound waves. Filters modify those sound waves.

levels.name: Filter
levels.text: This panel controls the settings for a Filter.

It also has a display which shows 2 things:
 1) Frequencies coming from the oscillator
2) and how they are being modified by the filter.
Push play on the sequencer to see the incoming frequencies displayed.
The filter give us control over the amplitude of all these incoming frequencies. From the fundamental to all the harmonics.
It has two different variables: Cutoff and Resonance.

All frequencies below the cutoff have their amplitudes preserved. 

Frequencies above the cutoff have their amplitudes reduced.
Resonance is a setting that can boost the frequencies that are at and around the cutoff.

Above the cutoff -> amplitude reduced

Near the cutoff -> amplitude boosted

Below the cutoff -> amplitude preserved
Push play on the sequencer and listen to how the sound changes as you adjust the filter's settings.

Quick metric unit recap:
kilo = 1000
Hz = Hertz
kHz = kiloHertz
20 kHz = 20,000 Hertz
Notice that the distance from 60Hz to 600Hz looks like the same distance from 600Hz to 6kHz.
This is because the Filter uses something called a logarithmic scale. This method of displaying frequencies is very common in sound design.
As you explore all these controls, there is an experiment I want you to try.

Set the controls to these settings: 
- cutoff to 20kHz
- resonance to 0%
- octave to 0
- semitone to 0
- amp to 1.00
Now play some notes and watch what frequencies are displayed in the filter.

Keep exploring as much as you want.

If you need to revisit a topic, use the selector above to visit different levels.

Congrats! You've completed Ravakele: Journey Into Sound

The next part of your sound design adventure is Ravakele: Descent into Madness
Loading this World resets all the synthesizer settings back to their starting values.
